newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: PAKISTAN PARLIAMENT PASSES ANTI-TERRORISM LAW.
newsitem.headline: PAKISTAN PARLIAMENT PASSES ANTI-TERRORISM LAW.

text.p: Pakistan's parliament, ignoring opposition protests, passed a draconian Anti-Terrorism Bill on Wednesday which gives the government sweeping new security powers, including the right to shoot suspects on sight and try them at short notice before special fast-track courts.

The opposition Pakistan People's Party (PPP), led by former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, walked out of the National Assembly (lower house) and the Senate (upper house) in protest when the controversial bill was passed by the two chambers.

The bill, an attempt to stop a wave of killings that has shaken Pakistan in the run-up to Thursday's golden jubilee celebration of 50 years of independence, was passed without any amendments to the government draft, thanks to large majorities Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif has in both houses.
Sharif had offered to incorporate any opposition proposal to improve the bill when the legislation was first moved in the 217-seat National Assembly.
But the PPP refused to be party to the bill after Sharif rejected their demand to put it off for two days, saying "it is a serious matter which needs timely action".
Opposition deputies said the law violated the fundamental rights of citizens and would be misused against political opponents.
But Sharif said the bill was aimed at terrorists and not against any politician or political party. "No politicking is involved in it,."he said.

More than 225 people have been killed in a feud involving rival wings of an ethnic party in Karachi so far this year, while a vendetta between militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem factions has cost about 140 lives, mostly in Punjab province.

"There is a spate of terrorist activities and commission of heinous offences in Pakistan," said the bill proposed by Interior Minister Shujaat Hussain. "It is necessary that appropriate administrative and judicial measures are adopted."
The bill, which now needs only the formality of presidential assent to become law, will let the federal or provincial governments call in armed forces to help civilian authorities.
It will authorise policemen, or soldiers deployed in such cases, to fire on anyone committing, or believed to be about to commit, a "terrorist" offence.
Security forces will also be allowed to arrest suspects, search premises and seize weapons or anything else used or likely to be used in a terrorist offence, without a warrant.

The bill prescribes the death penalty for any terrorist whose action has caused a death, and sentences of seven years and life imprisonment otherwise. It bans "acts intended or likely to stir up sectarian hatred" and punishes their perpetrators with up to seven years in jail.

The bill enables the government to set up special courts, with police required to complete investigation of cases within seven working days. The courts would have to decide such cases within a further seven days with a similar period for an appellate tribunal to judge appeals against such verdicts.
The federal or provincial governments could declare any association unlawful "in the interest of public order".
Sharif's government has come under intense pressure to halt the bloodletting in Karachi and Punjab, with many newspaper commentators calling for sectarian groups to be banned.
Sharif told foreign correspondents earlier on Wednesday that the new law did not provide for any new penalties and was intended to bring terrorists speedily to trial.
"The problem of sectarianism is continuing for some time in Pakistan and it is a very serious problem, and under the garb of the religion, people are killng each other."

He said many alleged terrorists had been arrested by police but had not been tried "for quite a long time" because of the existing legal procedures. "So when punishments are not awarded to these terrorists, then of course, you can't stop terrorism."
